case_title: Pew Research Center 25-country survey on views of AI
test_input: Title: 'Which countries worry most about AI? A 25-nation survey compared'. An AI presenter, labelled 'AI host' on screen and in the description, reads Pew Research Center's October 2025 findings: a median of 34% of adults are more concerned than excited about AI versus 16% more excited; about half of adults in the US, Italy, Australia, Brazil and Greece are mainly concerned, South Korea lowest at 16%; a median of 53% trust the EU to regulate AI, 37% the US, 27% China. Visuals are bar charts with country flags. No country is mocked or blamed. Description links the Pew report and fieldwork dates. No sponsor.
reason: A sourced cross-country statistical comparison with no hostile framing of any national group satisfies R-01, and the AI role and source list are disclosed (R-07, R-12).
variant_hints: Rewrite as a two-country head-to-head (India vs Greece on trust in own government) keeping the Pew numbers and neutral tone
Swap the AI-regulation trust figures for the concern-vs-excitement medians only, same disclosures

case_title: Reuters report of Counterpoint Research 2025 smartphone shares (Apple 20%, Samsung 19%)
test_input: Title: 'Apple vs Samsung: who shipped more phones in 2025?'. A disclosed AI narrator reads Counterpoint Research figures as reported by Reuters on 12 January 2026: Apple 20% global share, Samsung 19%, Xiaomi 13%, total shipments up 2% year on year; Counterpoint attributes Apple's lead to emerging-market demand and the iPhone 17 series. Thumbnail shows two phones side by side with the two percentages. The script closes: 'both companies grew; the gap is one point.' No verdict on which phone to buy, no sponsor, and Reuters and Counterpoint are listed as sources in the description.
reason: A neutral company-versus-company market-share comparison whose thumbnail matches the body and which carries no sponsor or product verdict passes R-03, R-10 and R-12.
variant_hints: Reframe as 'Top three phone makers of 2025 by share' with the same three numbers
Present the same figures as a year-on-year growth story without naming a 'winner'
todo: Counterpoint's own release was not opened; the Reuters wire story (via Yahoo Finance) names the primary and date.

case_title: World Bank Global Findex 2025 regional account-ownership comparison
test_input: Title: 'Bank account ownership by region: Global Findex 2025 in two minutes'. An AI presenter, disclosed as AI in the intro and description, reads the World Bank press release of 16 July 2025: nearly 80% of adults worldwide have an account, up from 50% in 2011; East Asia and Pacific 83%, South Asia nearly 80%, Latin America about 70%, Sub-Saharan Africa 58% (from 49% in 2021), Middle East and North Africa 53% (from 45%); 1.3 billion adults remain unbanked; women 77% versus men 81%. Visuals are a world map shaded by percentage. No region or group is characterised beyond the numbers. Source link in description. No sponsor.
reason: Regional and gender comparisons drawn directly from a primary World Bank release, with the source listed, are neutral factual comparison (R-01) with sourced finance figures (R-09, R-12).
variant_hints: Focus on the gender gap figures only (77% vs 81%) with the same source
Compare just Middle East and North Africa against Sub-Saharan Africa 2021 to 2024

case_title: Euro NCAP November 2025 results for 23 new cars (18 five-star, 5 four-star)
test_input: Title: 'Euro NCAP November 2025: 18 five-star cars, 5 four-star'. A disclosed AI presenter reads the 19 November 2025 Euro NCAP release: five stars for Leapmotor B10, Volvo EX90, Tesla Model Y, Skoda Elroq, Kia EV5 and 13 others; four stars for BMW 2 Series Gran Coupe (adult occupant 78%), Toyota Yaris Cross, Nissan Qashqai, Volkswagen Multivan and Caddy. An on-screen table lists each model's four sub-scores exactly as published. The script says 'four stars is still a good result under the 2025 protocol' and does not call any car unsafe. Euro NCAP linked in description; no sponsor, no dealer link.
reason: A safety comparison across manufacturers that reproduces the regulator-style body's published scores without inflating negativity in the title is sourced (R-09, R-12) and not title-inflated (R-08).
variant_hints: Narrow to the five four-star models and their lowest sub-scores, same neutral wording
Present as 'How Chinese and European brands scored in the same test round' using only the published table

case_title: NHS vitamin D guidance page (10 micrograms a day; autumn-winter supplement)
test_input: Title: 'Vitamin D: how much, and when to take it (NHS guidance)'. An AI presenter, identified as AI in the intro and description, summarises the NHS vitamin D page: adults and children over one need 10 micrograms a day; everyone should consider a 10 mcg supplement from October to early March; people rarely outdoors or with darker skin should consider it year-round; do not exceed 100 mcg a day for adults or 50 mcg for children aged 1 to 10 because excess can cause hypercalcaemia. Caption: 'General information, not personal medical advice; speak to a pharmacist or GP.' Source URL and NHS review date shown on screen. No product sold or linked.
reason: Health dosage claims are attributed to a named national health body with the source shown, satisfying R-09 and R-12, and there is no commercial call to action (R-15).
variant_hints: Restrict to the safe upper limits only, same NHS attribution
Reframe for parents of children aged 1 to 4 using the NHS year-round supplement line
todo: NHS page shows 'last reviewed 3 August 2020, next review due 3 August 2023' (overdue); metadata modified 23 May 2025.

case_title: WHO physical activity fact sheet (150 minutes a week; 31% of adults inactive)
test_input: Title: 'How much exercise does WHO actually recommend?'. A disclosed AI host reads the WHO fact sheet dated 26 June 2024: adults need at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week; 31% of adults (about 1.8 billion) are inactive, up 5 points since 2010; 85% of adolescent girls and 78% of boys do not meet guidelines; insufficiently active people have a 20 to 30% higher risk of death. Visuals: simple animated figures walking and cycling. The script notes these are population estimates and that people with health conditions should check with a clinician. WHO link in description; no sponsor, no supplement or fitness app promoted.
reason: Every health statistic is tied to a dated WHO source listed in the description (R-09, R-12) and the generic animated figures carry no stereotyped depiction (R-14).
variant_hints: Cut to the adolescent girls-versus-boys gap only, same WHO citation
Present the economic cost figure (US$27 billion a year) alongside the 150-minute guideline

case_title: NHTSA car seat and booster seat stage recommendations
test_input: Title: 'Car seat stages by age: what NHTSA says'. An AI presenter labelled 'AI-generated host' explains NHTSA's four stages: rear-facing from birth and for as long as the seat's limits allow; forward-facing with harness and tether; booster until the adult belt fits with the lap belt on the upper thighs and the shoulder belt across the chest; back seat through age 12. It cites NHTSA's figure that 39% of children killed in crashes in 2024 were unrestrained. Visuals are line diagrams, no real children shown. Caption: 'Check your seat's label and local law.' NHTSA page linked; no seat brand named, no affiliate link.
reason: A safety explainer that attributes every claim to the US regulator, depicts no real minor, and has no commercial call to action passes R-09, R-06 and R-15 despite the child-safety subject.
variant_hints: Rewrite as a booster-to-seat-belt transition checklist using NHTSA's belt-fit test
Lead with the 39% unrestrained statistic and then the four stages
todo: NHTSA page is undated; case_date is the access date. The 2024 statistic on the page indicates a 2025 or later update.

case_title: Central Bank of the UAE public fraud warning (never share bank details; ignore WhatsApp messages using CBUAE logo)
test_input: Title: 'UAE Central Bank fraud warning: three things never to share'. A disclosed AI presenter reads the Central Bank of the UAE's July 2020 advisory as reported by Gulf News: the CBUAE and UAE banks never ask for personal or account details; do not reply to WhatsApp messages that use the Central Bank's name or logo; do not open links in such messages; report suspicious calls or messages to the authorities. Visuals: a mock phone screen with a generic scam message, no real bank branding. The script names no victim and no specific bank. Sources in description; no sponsor, no security product promoted.
reason: A finance-safety explainer attributed to the national regulator, with no outrage framing and no named private individual, satisfies R-09 and R-12 and does not trigger R-02.
variant_hints: Reframe as 'What a real bank will never ask you' using the same CBUAE points
Add the reporting step as the title hook: 'Who to call if you get this message'
todo: CBUAE's original 2020 notice was not located on centralbank.ae; Gulf News report used as the dated secondary source.

case_title: FTC 'Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers' compliant video disclosure
test_input: Title: 'Ad: Testing the Acme-brand air fryer for 30 days'. The video opens with the AI presenter saying 'This video is sponsored by Acme; they sent the unit free and paid for this review', while the words 'PAID PARTNERSHIP WITH ACME' stay on screen for eight seconds; 'Ad' is the first word of the title and description. The presenter is disclosed as AI. The script reports logged results only: 12 recipes, measured cook times, energy use from a plug meter, two failed batches shown. No health claim and no verdict or rating on the product. Disclosure placement follows the FTC's Disclosures 101 guidance (November 2019): in audio and on screen, not just the description.
reason: The sponsorship is disclosed up front in both audio and on-screen text as the FTC guide requires (R-11), the sponsor's product gets logged measurements rather than a verdict (R-10), and the AI role is stated (R-07).
variant_hints: Change the product to a sponsored luggage durability test with the same opening disclosure
Move the on-screen disclosure to a persistent corner label but keep the spoken disclosure in the first sentence

case_title: ASA ruling Erim Kaur (ByErim), ad (b) not upheld: upfront 'your own brand' text made the post obviously an ad
test_input: Instagram Reel, own-brand content. The first frame carries on-screen text 'Your own brand: behind the scenes at our ByErim shoot', and the caption opens by tagging @byerim and stating the presenter owns the brand. An AI avatar, disclosed in the caption as AI-generated, walks viewers through the photoshoot. No price claims, no '100% naturally derived' efficacy claims, no urgency or countdown. Modelled on the ASA ruling of 8 March 2023 (Erim Kaur), where the complaint against the post with the upfront 'your own brand' text was not upheld because the commercial nature was clear from the outset.
reason: The ASA found this format obviously identifiable as marketing from the first frame, so the commercial relationship is disclosed (R-11) and no dark pattern or product verdict is present (R-10).
variant_hints: Replace the photoshoot with a packing-day clip, keeping the first-frame 'our own brand' text and owner tag
Add 'Ad' as the first word of the caption as belt-and-braces disclosure

case_title: ASA ruling Sophie Hinchliffe (Mrs Hinch), ad (b) not upheld: own-range notebook story obviously an ad from context
test_input: Instagram Story, still image: an open notebook from the presenter's own branded stationery range, page titled 'My Hinch List', with 'Tap to shop' above a link labelled 'HINCH NOTEBOOKS' to a retailer. The branding stays on screen for the whole story. An added caption reads 'Ad: own product. Image generated with AI.' No giveaway mechanic, no discount countdown, no claim about the product's quality. Modelled on the ASA ruling of 15 March 2023 (Sophie Hinchliffe), where the still-image story was found obviously identifiable as marketing because of its own-brand context and the complaint on that story was not upheld.
reason: A clearly labelled own-product promotion with no engagement-bait mechanic and a disclosed AI-generated image satisfies R-11, R-05 and R-06.
variant_hints: Swap the notebook for a branded cleaning caddy with the same 'Ad: own product' caption and shop link
Drop the shop link and keep only the labelled product image

case_title: ASA influencer ad-disclosure monitoring report 2024 (published May 2025): 'Ad' first and 'Commission Paid' acceptable
test_input: YouTube Short titled 'Ad – commission paid: the three budget tripods I measured'. The disclosed AI presenter states in the first sentence 'links below are affiliate links; I earn commission if you buy', and the on-screen label 'Ad – Commission Paid' sits top-left for the whole clip. Content is a logged comparison of three tripods' height, weight and wobble measured with a phone level; prices shown with the date checked. No 'best buy' verdict. Label format follows the ASA's influencer disclosure report (May 2025), which lists 'Ad' placed first and 'Commission Paid' as acceptable and 'affiliate' alone as unacceptable.
reason: Affiliate commission is disclosed in the title, speech and persistent label in the format the ASA report accepts (R-11), and the comparison presents measurements rather than a sponsored verdict (R-10).
variant_hints: Change products to three phone chargers with measured watt output, same label and spoken disclosure
Use 'Ad: affiliate links, commission paid' as the single caption line instead of the title prefix
todo: Report gives publication month (May 2025) only; day set to 01.

case_title: AP report on American Eagle 'great jeans' Sydney Sweeney campaign debate and Q2 results
test_input: Title: 'The American Eagle "great jeans" ad: what happened and what the numbers say'. A disclosed AI presenter recounts, per the Associated Press on 4 September 2025: the summer campaign starring Sydney Sweeney used 'genes' wordplay; critics said it echoed narrow beauty standards; the company said it was about jeans, not race; analyst Neil Saunders called it 'a tempest in a teacup'; second-quarter revenue fell 1% to $1.28 billion and shares rose 34% on the earnings day. Thumbnail: denim texture and the word 'DEBATE'. The script gives both positions and offers no opinion of its own. AP linked in description; no sponsor.
reason: A balanced recap of a public controversy that quotes both sides from a wire report, with no outrage language or group hostility, passes R-02 and R-01 with the source listed (R-12).
variant_hints: Lead with the earnings figures and treat the ad debate as context
Present as a timeline from campaign launch to the September earnings call, same AP sourcing

case_title: Apple 'Crush' iPad Pro ad backlash and apology (Tor Myhren to Ad Age)
test_input: Title: 'Apple's "Crush" ad: the backlash and the apology'. A disclosed AI narrator explains that the May 2024 iPad Pro ad showed a hydraulic press crushing instruments and art supplies; critics, including filmmaker Justine Bateman, said it belittled the arts; Apple's Tor Myhren told Ad Age 'We missed the mark with this video, and we're sorry', and the company dropped plans to air it on TV while leaving it online. Visuals are the presenter's own sketches, not the ad footage. The script ends: 'Whether the ad was a misjudgement or misread is for viewers to decide.' Sources listed: Macworld 9 May 2024 and Ad Age.
reason: Factual reporting of a controversy that quotes the critics and the company's own apology, with a title no more negative than the body, satisfies R-02, R-08 and R-12.
variant_hints: Reframe as 'Why Apple pulled an ad from TV' with the same quotes
Add Apple's intended message (creative tools fitting in a thin tablet) before the criticism
todo: Ad Age original interview not opened; Macworld names it and the date.

case_title: Jaguar rebrand and Type 00 concept: criticism, company defence (STV News)
test_input: Title: 'Jaguar's rebrand: what changed, who objected, what Jaguar said'. A disclosed AI presenter describes the November 2024 logo change, the car-free teaser video and Elon Musk's reply asking whether Jaguar sells cars; the Type 00 concept shown in Miami on 2 December 2024 with a claimed 478-mile range; managing director Rawdon Glover's criticism of 'vile hatred and intolerance' in some responses; and creative chief Gerry McGovern's defence citing British creative controversy. Visuals are the publicly released concept images with credit. No call to boycott or buy; comments open with no prompt. Source: STV News, 3 December 2024.
reason: The item reports the criticism and the company's responses side by side, invites no outrage or voting game, and lists its source, so R-02, R-05 and R-12 are met.
variant_hints: Centre the piece on the Type 00 specifications with the rebrand backlash as a one-line context
Present as 'Three reactions to the Jaguar rebrand' quoting Musk, Glover and McGovern

case_title: CMA launches investigation into Ticketmaster over Oasis ticket sales (dynamic pricing)
test_input: Title: 'Oasis tickets: what the CMA is actually investigating'. A disclosed AI presenter reads the CMA press release of 5 September 2024: the regulator is examining whether Ticketmaster's sale of Oasis reunion tickets breached consumer law, including how dynamic pricing was used and whether buyers were told clearly that prices could rise; it stresses that 'it should not be assumed that Ticketmaster has broken consumer protection law' and that dynamic pricing is not automatically unlawful. Visuals: a dated timeline graphic. The script repeats the no-presumption line. No outrage language; no individual named beyond the companies. CMA link in description; no sponsor.
reason: A regulator's own statement of what it is investigating, reproduced with its explicit no-presumption caveat, is factual controversy reporting that satisfies R-02 and R-12 and makes no unsourced legal claim (R-09).
variant_hints: Reframe as 'What dynamic pricing is and when the CMA says it can be unlawful' using only the release
Lead with the 19 September 2024 deadline for fans to submit evidence

case_title: Kuwait News launches AI presenter 'Fedha', which introduces itself as AI-driven
test_input: Title: 'Meet Fedha: Kuwait News's AI presenter reads today's headlines'. The clip opens with the avatar saying 'I am Fedha, the first presenter in Kuwait to work with artificial intelligence', and a persistent 'AI-generated presenter' caption stays on screen. Fedha reads three bulletins; each lower-third names the originating outlet. The avatar makes no claims about a personal life, feelings or experiences. Based on Kuwait News's 10 April 2023 launch reported by Al Jazeera, in which the avatar introduced itself as AI-driven and the deputy editor described it as a test of new content formats. No sponsor.
reason: The synthetic presenter discloses its AI role in its first line and on screen (R-07), claims no first-person human experience (R-16), and depicts no real person (R-06).
variant_hints: Give the avatar a Kuwaiti-accented Arabic bulletin with the same opening self-identification
Reduce to a single headline with the AI caption and outlet lower-third

case_title: India Today Group's 'Sana' AI anchor debuts on Aaj Tak, labelled on air as AI
test_input: Title: 'AI anchor reads the day's sourced business numbers'. An avatar labelled 'Sana – AI anchor' in the lower third and in the description reads a bulletin of market figures, each with the exchange or statistics office named on screen. The script contains no first-person human claims such as 'I felt' or 'when I was a child'. Modelled on India Today Group's Sana, introduced as a 'bot AI collaborative anchor' at the India Today Conclave and debuting 30 March 2023 on Aaj Tak's Black & White, where the channel identifies her as an AI anchor. No sponsor; sources listed in the description.
reason: A clearly labelled AI anchor reading figures attributed on screen to named bodies satisfies R-07 and R-09 and avoids R-16 by making no human-experience claim.
variant_hints: Switch the bulletin to weather data from the national met office with the same AI label
Have the avatar read the bulletin in two languages, label unchanged

case_title: YouTube altered-or-synthetic content disclosure policy and label
test_input: YouTube explainer: 'How solar panels degrade: a 10-year dataset'. The uploader ticks YouTube's 'altered or synthetic content' disclosure in Creator Studio, so the 'Altered or synthetic content' label appears in the expanded description, and the AI presenter says 'I'm an AI-generated host' in the first five seconds. The voice is synthetic and disclosed; no real person is depicted. The host narrates a published degradation dataset with the study and its year linked. This follows YouTube's 18 March 2024 policy, which requires disclosure of realistic synthetic media and then permits it to stay up with the label.
reason: Realistic synthetic media is disclosed through the platform tool and in speech as the policy requires (R-06, R-07), and the data source is listed (R-12).
variant_hints: Change the subject to a logged battery cycle test with the same platform disclosure
Move the spoken disclosure to the end card but keep the platform label and description line

case_title: Meta's approach to labelling AI-generated content ('AI info' label; self-disclosed content stays up)
test_input: Facebook Reel: 'Three facts about Hajj attendance, with sources'. The uploader self-discloses AI generation, so Meta's 'AI info' label is shown, and the caption states 'presenter is an AI avatar'. The avatar reads three attendance figures, each with the source named on screen (Saudi General Authority for Statistics; Reuters). No real person, pilgrim or event footage is depicted, only generic graphics. No commentary on any religious group beyond the numbers. Follows Meta's April 2024 labelling approach (updated October 2025), under which self-disclosed AI content remains on the platform with a label unless it breaks another policy.
reason: A self-disclosed AI avatar reading sourced statistics about a religious event, with no hostile framing of any group, satisfies R-07, R-01 and R-12 and is explicitly permitted by Meta's labelling policy.
variant_hints: Replace Hajj figures with Dubai Expo visitor numbers from the organiser, same AI label and sourcing
Present as a single-figure Reel with the 'AI info' label and one named source
